en: Now,
one
last important decision you need to make
when building an AI agent yourself
is which building blocks you want to
support. You learned about them before, that
an agent is all about that agentic loop and
that you, for example, of course, need a
model as a brain, but you need to decide
which model,
that you typically have system instructions
and you need to decide which specific
instructions your agent needs, and that you
need tools and you, guess what, need to
decide which Which tools your agent needs to
do its job. And these are all questions
we'll get back to once we build our own
agents in the next sections.
But then there also are optional building
blocks. You need to decide whether you want
your agent to execute tools in a sandbox,
for example.
You need to decide whether you want to
support agent skills, that standard you
learned about, if you want your agent to
support that standard, because if you build
it on your own, it does not magically
support that standard. Standard, you must
make it supported. It's a standard so that
agents can implement it and support it. But
if you decide to not implement it, then your
agent, despite that standard existing,
doesn't know anything about it and doesn't
support it. There is no magical connection
there. So that is a decision you need to
make, and we'll also dive into that.
You'll also have to decide if your agent
should have a memory feature. I showed you
the memory feature of Claude Cowork earlier,
but that's not a given. Not all agents have
that, and you need to decide if your agent,
for the job it's meant to do, if it needs
that.
For workflows, this does of course not
matter. If it's an AI workflow, you will
have to choose a model and you will need
instructions. But per definition, since
workflows are deterministic, it's not about
tools, not about skills, not about memory or
any of that.
